2 2. According to the prosecution case, the respondent no.2 lodged an FIR on the allegations that she got married to Kuldeep Parashar on 3.3.2020. The respondent no.2 is an educated lady and is a Software Engineer and is working in CGI Company at Bangalore. Kuldeep Parashar was also working in the same company; whereas applicants no.5 and 6 namely; Prashant Vajpayi and Smt.Priyanka Vajpayi were also working in SAP Company at Bangalore. During the discussions for marriage, the applicants no.1, 2, 3 and 4 expressed that the talks of marriage of Kuldeep Parashar is going on at some different place, where an offer has been made to give Rs.10,00,000/- and a big car apart from the household articles, therefore, the parents of the respondent no.2 should also give the same dowry in the marriage. Accordingly, it was alleged that the parents of the respondent no.2 had given Rs.10,00,000/- in cash, gold chain of 2 tola, gold neckless of 2 tola, gold earring, etc. and also gave the household articles like fridge, washing machine, double bed, dressing table, sitting table,
water purifier, kitchen set, steel utensils etc.,worth Rs.3,50,000/-. The details of the total jewellery given at the time of marriage etc. and the other gifts were also mentioned in the FIR. While they were returning back after the marriage was performed, they stopped at a hotel for having food where the applicants no.1 and 3 were discussing that they were expecting a big car, which has not been given. She stayed in her matrimonial house for 7 days and during this period, the applicants no.1 to 4 suggested to the respondent no.2 that it would not be proper to keep so much of jewellery in Bangalore because both of them are working , therefore, the respondent no.2 should leave her ornaments with the applicants no.1 to 4 and whenever she would ask for the same, the jewellery would be returned back. Even the applicants no.5 and 6 also assured that the jewellery would be returned as soon as it is required. Therefore, by relying upon the assurance given by the applicants,
the respondent no.2 left her jewellery with applicants no.1 to 4. Thereafter, the respondent no.2 and her husband came to Gadarwara on the festival of Holi and the applicants no.1 to 4 also came to Gadarwara and they resided there for 2 days. During this period it was alleged by the applicants no.1 to 4 that the respondent no.2 has not handed over the entire jewellery and since they would be residing in Bangalore, therefore, the respondent no.2 must handover the entire jewellery, which would be in the safe custody of the applicants. Accordingly, with an assurance to return the jewellery, the applicants no.1 to 4 took the entire gold ornaments from the respondent no.2. When the respondent no.2 went to Bangalore then it is alleged that her husband started alleging that they would be required to stay in a rented house and since he has no money for payment of advance and earnest money, therefore, the respondent no.2 should take a house on rent and accordingly, the respondent no.2 paid Rs.2,00,000/- towards the advance rent and the earnest money and also purchased the household articles worth Rs.5,00,000/-. After the rented house was taken, the behavior of Kuldeep Parashar changed all of sudden and started alleging that the wish of his family members was that they would get a big car, but a big car has not been given and dowry as per their wishes, has also not been given. When it was objected by the respondent no.2 that her parents have already given sufficient dowry as per their financial capabilities, then her husband started quarrelling with her and also assaulted her and alleged and unless and until a big car is given, he will not keep her with him and he was also not visiting the house in the night. When this fact was informed by the respondent no.2 to applicants on phone and told about her difficulties then all of them stated that since her parents have not given the dowry, as per the wishes of in-laws and has also not given the big car, therefore, she should take a big car from her parent, otherwise she is free to take divorce and thereafter the in-laws stopped talking to the respondent no.2. The husband of the respondent no.2 got the locks of the house changed and kept the key with him and on one day Jagdish Parashar vs The Of Madhya Pradesh on 15 April, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/184044456/
3 the respondent no.2 was made to wait for 4 to 5 hours. Even her husband did not bring the key and under compulsion the respondent no.2 was compelled to go to house of her sister. They stayed in the rented house for 2 months and during this period, her husband was consistently quarrelling with her and was insisting that she should go back to her parental house and should fulfill the demands, 
otherwise he would perform second marriage and in case if any objection is raised, then she would be killed. They are the residents of UP and nobody would be able to find out the whereabouts of her dead body also. On 28.6.2020 her husband vacated the house in her absence and shifted to Lalitpur along with the entire household articles and since then he has no contact with the respondent no.2. 
With great difficulty the respondent no.2 succeeded in talking to her husband then he specifically narrated that their intention was to extort the money from them and they have successfully done so and, therefore, the respondent no.2 may do whatever she wants. Although the respondent no.2 gave an information of this incident to the police but since she was not interested in severing the marital ties, therefore, she did not narrate the incidents in detail. It was alleged that her parents are not in a position to give a big car; whereas her husband and her in-laws are demanding dowry. They are again and again are sending messages to the relatives that either their demand should be fulfilled;
otherwise they have already deserted the respondent no.2. During her stay in her parental home, the applicants are harassing her mentally and she has an apprehension that they would permanently severe the relationship and accordingly an FIR was lodged. 
3. Challenging the FIR, it is submitted by counsel for the applicants that it is well established principle of law that the allegations must be clear and specific. The allegations, which have been made against the applicants, are vague, omnibus and general in nature and in the light of judgment passed by the Supreme Court in the case of Kans Raj v. State of Punjab, reported in (2000) 5 SCC 207, Monju Roy v. State of W.B., (2015) 13 SCC 693, Chandralekha & Ors. v. State of Rajasthan &
Anr. reported in 2013 (1) UC 155, Geeta Mehrotra Vs. State of U.P. reported in (2012) 10 SCC 741,
Preeti Gupta Vs. State of Jharkhand, reported in (2010) 7 SCC 667, the prosecution of the applicants is unwarranted. It is further submitted that there is a delay of 8 months in lodging the FIR. The husband of the respondent no.2 had filed an application under section 13 of the Hindu Marriage Act and the notices were served on the respondent no.2 on 29.3.2021 and by way of counter-blast, the FIR in question has been lodged on 22.5.2021. Even if the entire allegations are read, no offence under sections 498- A, 506-II and 406 of IPC is made out. 
4. Per contra, the application is vehemently opposed by the counsel for the State as well as the counsel for the respondent no.2. It is submitted by Shri Saurabh Bhushan Shrivastava that the police has already filed a chargesheet and charges have been framed and it is well established principle of law that even if there is a grave suspicion to the effect that the accused might have committed an offence, then it is sufficient to frame the charges. 
5. To buttress his contention, the counsel for respondent no.2 has relied upon a judgment passed by the Supreme Court in the case of State of Rajasthan Vs. Fatehkaran Mehdu, reported in (2017) 3 SCC 198 and Soma Chakravarty Vs. State through CBI, reported in (2007) 5 SCC 403.
6. In reply, it is submitted by counsel for the applicants that merely because the charges have been framed, it would not mean that the application for quashment of proceedings would become Jagdish Parashar vs The Of Madhya Pradesh on 15 April, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/184044456/
4 infructuous. 
7. Heard the learned counsel for the parties. 
Delay in lodging the FIR 8. According to the respondent no.2, the marriage was performed on 4.3.2020 and her husband deserted her permanently on 28.6.2020; whereas the FIR was lodged with delay of 8 months. 
9. The moot question for consideration is as to whether the FIR, which was lodged after a delay of 8 months, can be said to be bad, warranting the quashment of the proceedings as well as the FIR or not? 
10. As per the provisions of section 468 of CrPC, the period of limitation for taking cognizance is 3 years. The respondent no.2 was permanently deserted by her husband on 28.6.2020; whereas the FIR was lodged on 22.5.2021. Thus, it is clear that the FIR was lodged much within a period of 3 years and thus, it cannot be said that it is barred by time. 
11. Furthermore, it is clear from the FIR that the respondent no.2 has been compelled to live separately on account of non-fulfillment of demand of dowry. Compelling a woman to live separately on account of non-fulfillment of demand of dowry would certainly amount to cruelty. 
12. The Supreme Court in the case of Rupali Devi v. State of U.P., reported in (2019) 5 SCC 384 has held as under:-
"14. "Cruelty" which is the crux of the offence under Section 498-A IPC is defined in Black's Law Dictionary to mean "the intentional and malicious infliction of mental or physical suffering on a living creature, esp. a human; abusive treatment; outrage (abuse, inhuman treatment, indignity)". Cruelty can be both physical or mental cruelty. The impact on the mental health of the wife by overt acts on the part of the husband or his relatives; the mental stress and trauma of being driven away from the matrimonial home and her helplessness to go back to the same home for fear of being ill-treated are aspects that cannot be ignored while understanding the meaning of the expression "cruelty" appearing in Section 498- A of the Penal Code. The emotional distress or psychological effect on the wife, if not the physical injury, is bound to continue to traumatise the wife even after she leaves the matrimonial home and takes shelter at the parental home. Even if the acts of physical cruelty committed in the matrimonial house may have ceased and such acts do not occur at the parental home,
there can be no doubt that the mental trauma and the psychological distress caused by the acts of the husband including verbal exchanges, if any, that had compelled the wife to leave the matrimonial home and take shelter with her parents would continue to persist at the parental home. Mental cruelty borne out of physical cruelty or abusive and humiliating verbal exchanges would continue in the parental home even though there may not be any overt act of physical cruelty at such place."

5 13. This Court in the case of Amar Singh vs. Smt. Vimla decided on 22.06.2021 in Criminal Revision No.2376/2020 (Gwalior Bench) has held that compelling a married woman to live in her parental home amounts to cruelty. 
14. Thus, it is clear that even otherwise, it is clear from the FIR that the allegations of cruelty are continuous in nature. Therefore, the proceedings cannot be quashed on the ground of delay. 
15. The Supreme Court in the case of Skoda Auto Volkswagen (India) Private Limited. v. State of U.P. and others, reported in (2021) 5 SCC 95 has held that in a petition for quashing the FIR, the Court cannot go into disputed question of fact. The mere delay on the part of complainant in lodging the complaint cannot by itself be a ground to quash the FIR. The Court cannot embark upon an enquiry as to the reliability, correctness of the allegations made in FIR or in complaint and criminal proceedings can not be scuttled at initial stage. 
16. The Supreme Court in the case of Ravinder Kumar and another v. State of Punjab, reported in (2001) 7 SCC 690 has held that attack on prosecution cases on the ground of delay in lodging FIR has almost bogged down as a stereotyped redundancy in criminal cases. It is a recurring feature in most of the criminal cases that there would be some delay in furnishing the first information to the police. It has to be remembered that law has not fixed any time for lodging the FIR. Hence a delayed FIR is not illegal. Of course, a prompt and immediate lodging of FIR is ideal as that would give the prosecution a twin advantage i.e. firstly it affords commencement of the investigation without any time lapse and secondly that it expels the opportunity for any possible concoction of a false version. 
Even otherwise promptly lodged FIR is also not an unreserved guarantee for the genuineness of the version incorporated therein. There may be variety of genuine causes for FIR lodgement to get delayed. 
17. The Supreme Court in the case of Mohammad Wajid and another vs. State of U.P. and others,
reported in AIR 2023 SC 3784 has held that delay in registration of FIR, by itself cannot be a ground for quashing of FIR. 
18. Thus, it is clear that not only there is no delay in lodging the FIR, but even otherwise the delay by itself cannot be ground to quash the proceedings. 
Whether the FIR has been lodged by way of counter-blast to petition for divorce filed by her husband or not? 
19. It is the contention of the applicants that the FIR is by way of counter-blast as the same was lodged on 22.5.2021; whereas the notice of the divorce petition was received by the respondent no.2 on 29.3.2021. 
20. Considered the aforesaid submissions made by counsel for applicants. 
21. The moot question for consideration is as to whether the lodging of FIR after the receipt of notice of divorce can be said to be bad on account of counter-blast or not?

6 22. The Supreme Court in the case of Pratibha v. Rameshwari Devi, reported in (2007) 12 SCC 369 has held as under:-
"14. From a plain reading of the findings arrived at by the High Court while quashing the FIR, it is apparent that the High Court had relied on extraneous considerations and acted beyond the allegations made in the FIR for quashing the same in exercise of its inherent powers under Section 482 of the Code. We have already noted the illustrations enumerated in Bhajan Lal case [1992 Supp (1) SCC 335 : 1992 SCC (Cri)
426] and from a careful reading of these illustrations, we are of the view that the allegations emerging from the FIR are not covered by any of the illustrations as noted hereinabove. For example, we may take up one of the findings of the High Court as noted hereinabove. The High Court has drawn an adverse inference on account of the FIR being lodged on 31-12-2001 while the appellant was forced out of the matrimonial home on 25-5-2001. 
15. In our view, in the facts and circumstances of the case, the High Court was not justified in drawing an adverse inference against the appellant wife for lodging the FIR on 31-12-2001 on the ground that she had left the matrimonial home at least six months before that. This is because, in our view, the High Court had failed to appreciate that the appellant and her family members were, during this period,
making all possible efforts to enter into a settlement so that Respondent 2 husband would take her back to the matrimonial home. If any complaint was made during this period, there was every possibility of not entering into any settlement with Respondent 2 husband. 
16. It is pertinent to note that the complaint was filed only when all efforts to return to the matrimonial home had failed and Respondent 2 husband had filed a divorce petition under Section 13 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955. That apart, in our view,
filing of a divorce petition in a civil court cannot be a ground to quash criminal proceedings under Section 482 of the Code as it is well settled that criminal and civil proceedings are separate and independent and the pendency of a civil proceeding cannot bring to an end a criminal proceeding even if they arise out of the same set of facts. Such being the position, we are, therefore, of the view that the High Court while exercising its powers under Section 482 of the Code has gone beyond the allegations made in the FIR and has acted in excess of its jurisdiction and, therefore, the High Court was not justified in quashing the FIR by going beyond the allegations made in the FIR or by relying on extraneous considerations.
23. If the facts of the present case is considered, then it is clear that no married women would like to lodge the FIR immediately after suffering cruelty at the hands of in-laws for obvious reason that she would not like to destroy her marital life and the first attempt of a married woman would be to save her marital life under a hope and belief that with passage of time, the things would improve. Only when she realizes that the things are going from bad to worse and then if she decides to lodge an FIR about the cruelty meted out to her by her in-laws, then it cannot be said that it is bad being counter- Jagdish Parashar vs The Of Madhya Pradesh on 15 April, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/184044456/
7 blast to the divorce petition. 
24. Furthermore, it is well established principle of law that the findings recorded by the civil court are not binding on the criminal court and every proceeding has to be decided in accordance with the degree of proof as well as in accordance with the material, which would come on record. 
25. Under these circumstances, this Court is of the considered opinion that the FIR lodged by the respondent no.2 cannot be quashed on the ground that it was lodged by way of counter-blast to the divorce petition filed by her husband. 
Whether the allegations made in the FIR make out an offence under sections 498-A and 506-II of PC or not? 
Applicants no.1 to 4 26. The applicant no.1 namely Jagdish Parashar is the father-in- law, the applicant no.2 Smt. 
Abhilasha Parashar is the mother-in- law, the applicant no.3 Anand Parashar is the elder brother-in-law (Jeth) and the applicant no.4 Smt.Anya a.k.a.Priyanka is the wife of applicant no.3. 
All are residing in the same house at Lalitpur. 
27. This Court has already reproduced the contents of the FIR and it is clear that right from the day one after the marriage, the applicants no.1 to 4 had a grudge that the parents of the respondent no.2 has not given a big car as well as sufficient dowry as per their wishes. It is also clear from the FIR that even prior to the settlement of marriage, the applicants no.1 to 4 had raised a demand by alleging that the other party has agreed to give Rs.10,00,000/- and a big car apart from the household articles, therefore, the parents of the respondent no.2 should give the same in dowry. 
28. There are specific allegations that the applicants no.1 to 4 have kept the ornaments of the respondent no.2 with them on the pretext that since she is going to stay in Bangalore, therefore, it would not be safe for them to keep the ornaments with them. According to the FIR, the ornaments have not been returned back. 
29. The marriage took place on 3.3.2020 and the respondent no.2 was permanently deserted by her husband on 28.6.2020, Therefore, it is clear that the respondent no.2 had resided with her husband and her in-laws for approximately 3 months. Under these circumstances, it cannot be said that in absence of the dates, the allegations would be vague and omnibus. The entire incidents of cruelty took place within a period of 3  months. 
30. Further, there are specific allegations against the applicants no.1 to 4 that they have kept the ornaments of the respondent no.2, which have not been returned back. Therefore, prima facie an offence under section 406 of IPC is also made out. 
31. The Supreme Court in the case of Taramani Parakh Vs. State of Madhya Pradesh and Others reported in (2015) 11 SCC 260 has held as under:-

8 " 12. In Kailash Chandra Agrawal v. State of U.P. [Kailash Chandra Agrawal v. State of U.P., (2014) 16 SCC 551] , it was observed (SCC p. 553, paras 8-9):
"8. We have gone through the FIR and the criminal complaint. In the FIR, the appellants have not been named and in the criminal complaint they have been named without attributing any specific role to them. The relationship of the appellants with the husband of the complainant is distant. In Kans Raj v. State of Punjab [Kans Raj v.
State of Punjab, (2000) 5 SCC 207 : 2000 SCC (Cri) 935 : (2000) 3 SCR 662] it was observed (SCC p. 217, para 5):
"5. ... A tendency has, however, developed for roping in all relations of the in-laws of the deceased wives in the matters of dowry deaths which, if not discouraged, is likely to affect the case of the prosecution even against the real culprits. In their overenthusiasm and anxiety to seek conviction for maximum people, the parents of the deceased have been found to be making efforts for involving other relations which ultimately weaken the case of the prosecution even against the real accused as appears to have happened in the instant case." 
The Court has, thus, to be careful in summoning distant relatives without there being specific material. Only the husband, his parents or at best close family members may be expected to demand dowry or to harass the wife but not distant relations, unless there is tangible material to support allegations made against such distant relations. Mere naming of distant relations is not enough to summon them in the absence of any specific role and material to support such role. 
9. The parameters for quashing proceedings in a criminal complaint are well known. If there are triable issues, the Court is not expected to go into the veracity of the rival versions but where on the face of it, the criminal proceedings are abuse of Court's process, quashing jurisdiction can be exercised. Reference may be made to K. Ramakrishna v. State of Bihar [K. Ramakrishna v. State of Bihar, (2000) 8 SCC 547 : 2001 SCC (Cri) 27] , Pepsi Foods Ltd. v. Judicial Magistrate [Pepsi Foods Ltd. v. Judicial Magistrate, (1998) 5 SCC 749 :
1998 SCC (Cri) 1400] , State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal [State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal, 1992 Supp (1) SCC 335 :
1992 SCC (Cri) 426 : AIR 1992 SC 604] and Asmathunnisa v. State of A.P.
[Asmathunnisa v. State of A.P., (2011) 11 SCC 259 : (2011) 3 SCC (Cri) 159] "
13. In the present case, the complaint is as follows:
"Sir, it is submitted that I was married on 18- 11-2009 with Sidharath Parakh s/o Manak Chand Parakh r/o Sarafa Bazar in front of Radha Krishna Market, Gwalior according to the Hindu rites and customs. In the marriage my father had given gold and silver ornaments, cash amount and household goods according to his capacity.

9 After the marriage when I went to my matrimonial home, I was treated nicely by the members of the family. When on the second occasion I went to my matrimonial home, my husband, father-in-law and mother-in-law started harassing me for not bringing the dowry and started saying that I should bring from my father 25-30 tolas of gold and Rs 2,00,000 in cash and only then they would keep me in the house otherwise not. On account of this my husband also used to beat me and my father-in-law and my mother-in-law used to torture me by giving the taunts. In this connection I used to tell my father Kundanmal Oswal, my mother Smt Prem Lata Oswal, uncle Ashok Rai Sharma and uncle Ved Prakash Mishra from time to time. On 2-4-2010 the members of the family of my matrimonial home forcibly sent me to the house of my parents in Ganj Basoda along with my brother Deepak. They snatched my clothes and ornaments and kept with them. Since then till today my husband has been harassing me on the telephone and has not come to take me back. Being compelled, I have been moving this application before you. Sir, it is prayed that action be taken against husband Sidharath Parakh, my father-in-law Manak Chand Parakh and my mother-in-law Smt Indira Parakh for torturing me on account of demanding dowry."
14. From a reading of the complaint, it cannot be held that even if the allegations are taken as proved no case is made out. There are allegations against Respondent 2 and his parents for harassing the complainant which forced her to leave the matrimonial home. Even now she continues to be separated from the matrimonial home as she apprehends lack of security and safety and proper environment in the matrimonial home. The question whether the appellant has in fact been harassed and treated with cruelty is a matter of trial but at this stage, it cannot be said that no case is made out. Thus, quashing of proceedings before the trial is not permissible." 
32. Under these circumstances, this Court is of the considered opinion that sufficient material is available on record warranting the prosecution of the applicant no.1 Jagdish Parashar, the applicant no.2 Smt. Abhilasha Parashar, the applicant no.3 Anand Parashar and the applicant no.4 Smt.Anya a.k.a.Priyanka.
33. Accordingly, the application filed by the applicants no.1 to 4 for quashment of the FIR as well as for quashment of the criminal proceedings is hereby dismissed. 
34. Applicant No.6 Smt. Priyanka Vajpayi is the married sister-in- law of the respondent no.2;
whereas the applicant no.5 Prashant Vajpayi is husband of applicant no.6.
35. From the chargesheet itself, it is clear that Priyanka Vajpayi and Smt. Prashant Vajpayi are residents of Kanpur; whereas other in- laws of the respondent no.2 are residents of Lalitpur. For prosecuting the near and dear relatives of the husband of the complainant, it is necessary that the allegations must be clear and specific and omnibus, vague and general allegations are not sufficient to prosecute them.

10 36. If the FIR is considered, then it is clear that except assuring that the ornaments would be returned back, no other allegations have been made against the applicants no.5 and 6.
37. Another general allegation has been made that when the respondent no.2 informed the applicants no.5 and 6 on phone about the cruel behavior of the husband, then they also stated that since the dowry has not been given as per their wishes, therefore, either she should bring a big car or she should go for divorce. Since the respondent nos.5 and 6 are residing separately at Kanpur and according to the respondent no.2 that she informed the applicants no.5 and 6 on phone , then this Court is of the considered opinion that the allegations are omnibus, vague and general and are not sufficient for prosecution of applicant no.5 Prashant Vajpayi and applicant no.6 Smt.Priyanaka Vajpayi. 
38. Accordingly, the FIR No.394/2021, registered at Police Station Gadarwara, District Narsinghpur against the applicants no.5 and 6 for offences under sections 498-A, 506, 406 of IPC and under section 3/4 of Dowry Prohibition Act as well as the Criminal Case No.559/2021 pending in the Court of JMFC, Gadarwara, District Narsinghpur and the charges dated 11.5.2022 framed against them are quashed. 
39. Accordingly, application filed by applicant no.1 Jagdish Parashar, applicant no.2 Smt. Abhilasha Parashar, applicant no.3 Anand Parashar and applicant no.4 Smt.Anya a.k.a.Priyanka is hereby dismissed and their prosecution for offence under sections 498-A, 506-II, 406 of IPC and section 3/4 of Dowry Prohibition Act shall continue; whereas the application filed by the applicant no.5 Prashant Vajpayi and applicant no.6 Smt. Priyanka Vajpayi is hereby allowed.

Therefore, the proceedings cannot be quashed on the ground of delay.
15. The Supreme Court in the case of Skoda Auto Volkswagen (India) Private Limited. v. State of U.P. and others, reported in (2021) 5 SCC 95 has held that in a petition for quashing the FIR, the Court cannot go into disputed question of fact.
The mere delay on the part of complainant in lodging the complaint cannot by itself be a ground to quash the FIR.
The Court cannot embark upon an enquiry as to the reliability, correctness of the allegations made in FIR or in complaint and criminal proceedings can not be scuttled at initial stage.
Hence a delayed FIR is not illegal.
Of course, a prompt and immediate lodging of FIR is ideal as that would give the prosecution a twin advantage i.e. firstly it affords commencement of the investigation without any time lapse and secondly that it expels the opportunity for any possible concoction of a false version.

Even otherwise promptly lodged FIR is also not an unreserved guarantee for the genuineness of the version incorporated therein.
There may be variety of genuine causes for FIR lodgement to get delayed.
That apart, in our view,
filing of a divorce petition in a civil court cannot be a ground to quash criminal proceedings under Section 482 of the Code as it is well settled that criminal and civil proceedings are separate and independent and the pendency of a civil proceeding cannot bring to an end a criminal proceeding even if they arise out of the same set of facts.
Such being the position, we are, therefore, of the view that the High Court while exercising its powers under Section 482 of the Code has gone beyond the allegations made in the FIR and has acted in excess of its jurisdiction and, therefore, the High Court was not justified in quashing the FIR by going beyond the allegations made in the FIR or by relying on extraneous considerations.

24. Furthermore, it is well established principle of law that the findings recorded by the civil court are not binding on the criminal court and every proceeding has to be decided in accordance with the degree of proof as well as in accordance with the material, which would come on record.
